grammar.title: BE: affirmative and negative
grammar.explanation: Use be to identify people, say where they are from, and give basic information.
grammar.form: I am / You are / He is / She is / It is / We are / They are. Negative: am not, isn’t, aren’t. Contractions: I’m, you’re, he’s, she’s, it’s, we’re, they’re.
grammar.examples: I’m from Brazil. / She isn’t a teacher.
grammar.translation: Eu sou do Brasil. / Ela não é professora.
grammar.usage: Use be with a subject; do not add do/does to be in the present.
grammar.errorExplanation: The negative particle follows the correct form of be.

grammar.title: Subject pronouns
grammar.explanation: Use a subject pronoun instead of repeating a person or thing as the subject.
grammar.form: I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Use he for a man/boy, she for a woman/girl, it for a thing/animal when sex is irrelevant, we for “I + others”.
grammar.examples: Maria is a student. She is in class. / Tom and I are friends. We are friends.
grammar.translation: Maria é estudante. Ela está na aula. / Tom e eu somos amigos. Nós somos amigos.
grammar.usage: The subject pronoun normally comes before the verb.
grammar.errorExplanation: I is the subject form; me is the object form.

grammar.title: Possessive adjectives
grammar.explanation: Show who something belongs to; they come directly before a noun.
grammar.form: my, your, his, her, its, our, their + noun.
grammar.examples: This is my book. / Their teacher is nice.
grammar.translation: Este é meu livro. / O professor deles é simpático.
grammar.usage: Possessive adjectives do not change for plural nouns: my book, my books.
grammar.commonError: She is my sister. Her name is Ana. → She is my sister. She name is Ana.
grammar.errorExplanation: Use her before the noun name.

chunks.use: Ask for spelling of a name or word.
chunks.example: It’s Ribeiro. — How do you spell that?

chunks.meaning: Qual é seu endereço de e-mail?
chunks.example: What’s your email address?
chunks.translation: Qual é seu endereço de e-mail?

chunks.use: Ask someone to say something again.
chunks.example: Sorry, can you repeat that, please?
chunks.translation: Desculpe, pode repetir, por favor?

workbook.explanation: She takes is.

workbook.explanation: What is your last name?

grammar.title: Singular and plural nouns
grammar.explanation: Use singular nouns for one item and plural nouns for more than one.
grammar.form: Most nouns: +s (book/books). Endings -s, -sh, -ch, -x: +es. Consonant + y: y → ies. Irregular: man/men, woman/women, child/children.
grammar.examples: one watch, two watches / one child, three children
grammar.translation: um relógio, dois relógios / uma criança, três crianças
grammar.usage: Use a/an with a singular countable noun, not with a plural.
grammar.errorExplanation: Words ending in -ch generally take -es.

grammar.title: Adjectives and word order
grammar.explanation: Adjectives describe nouns and usually go before the noun or after be.
grammar.form: a + adjective + noun; subject + be + adjective. Adjectives do not take plural -s.
grammar.examples: It’s a small bag. / My shoes are comfortable.
grammar.translation: É uma bolsa pequena. / Meus sapatos são confortáveis.
grammar.usage: In English, adjectives do not agree in number or gender.
grammar.errorExplanation: The adjective remains unchanged.

grammar.title: Imperatives and let’s
grammar.explanation: Use imperatives for instructions; use let’s to suggest an activity together.
grammar.form: Base verb: Open the door. Negative: Don’t touch it. Let’s + base verb: Let’s go.
grammar.examples: Please sit down. / Let’s take a break.
grammar.translation: Por favor, sente-se. / Vamos fazer uma pausa.
grammar.usage: Use don’t + base verb for a negative command.
grammar.errorExplanation: Do not add to after don’t.

grammar.title: Simple present: affirmative and negative
grammar.explanation: Use the simple present for habits, routines and general facts.
grammar.form: I/you/we/they + base verb; he/she/it + verb-s. Negative: don’t/doesn’t + base verb.
grammar.examples: I work at home. / She doesn’t drive.
grammar.translation: Eu trabalho em casa. / Ela não dirige.
grammar.usage: After does/doesn’t, use the base verb without -s.
grammar.errorExplanation: Does carries the third-person marking.

grammar.title: Simple present questions
grammar.explanation: Use do/does to ask about routines, preferences and facts.
grammar.form: Do + I/you/we/they + base verb? Does + he/she/it + base verb? Short answers: Yes, I do. / No, she doesn’t.
grammar.examples: Do you like dogs? / Does he work nights?
grammar.translation: Você gosta de cães? / Ele trabalha à noite?
grammar.usage: Do not use do with be; be forms its own questions.
grammar.errorExplanation: The main verb remains in the base form.

grammar.title: Word order and question words
grammar.explanation: Question words request specific information and normally come before do/does.
grammar.form: What/Where/When/Why/Who/How + do/does + subject + base verb? Adverbs of frequency usually precede a main verb.
grammar.examples: Where do you work? / He usually gets up at seven.
grammar.translation: Onde você trabalha? / Ele geralmente se levanta às sete.
grammar.usage: With be, the adverb usually follows be: She is always early.
grammar.errorExplanation: Place do/does between the question word and subject.

vocabulary.translation: Ela vai ao trabalho de trem.
Meu colega de trabalho ajuda muito.
Eles têm dois animais de estimação.

grammar.title: Possessive ’s and Whose
grammar.explanation: Use ’s to show belonging and whose to ask about ownership.
grammar.form: person + ’s + noun (Anna’s phone). Whose + noun + be…? Whose is this? Whose are those?
grammar.examples: This is my brother’s car. / Whose keys are these?
grammar.translation: Este é o carro do meu irmão. / De quem são estas chaves?
grammar.usage: Use apostrophe-s for a singular owner; whose asks “de quem”.
grammar.errorExplanation: Who’s means who is; whose is possessive.

grammar.title: Prepositions of time and place
grammar.explanation: Use in/on/at to locate events in time and items/people in places.
grammar.form: Time: at 7:00, on Monday, in July / in the morning. Place: at work, in a room, on a table.
grammar.examples: I start work at nine. / The photo is on the wall.
grammar.translation: Começo a trabalhar às nove. / A foto está na parede.
grammar.usage: Learn common collocations; time prepositions do not translate one-to-one from Portuguese.
grammar.errorExplanation: Use on with days.

grammar.title: Adverbs of frequency
grammar.explanation: Describe how often routines happen.
grammar.form: always, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never + main verb. With be: be + adverb.
grammar.examples: We usually eat together. / She is never late.
grammar.translation: Nós geralmente comemos juntos. / Ela nunca se atrasa.
grammar.usage: Place the adverb before most main verbs, but after be.
grammar.commonError: He goes always to bed early.
grammar.correction: He always goes to bed early.
grammar.errorExplanation: Frequency adverbs normally precede the main verb.

workbook.explanation: Twice a month is the usual phrase.

grammar.title: Can / can’t
grammar.explanation: Use can for ability or possibility and can’t for inability or impossibility.
grammar.form: Subject + can/can’t + base verb. Questions: Can + subject + base verb? Short answers: Yes, I can. / No, I can’t.
grammar.examples: She can drive. / Can you help me?
grammar.translation: Ela sabe dirigir. / Você pode me ajudar?
grammar.usage: Can is followed by the base form without to.
grammar.errorExplanation: Never put to after can.

grammar.title: Present continuous
grammar.explanation: Use for actions happening now or around now.
grammar.form: am/is/are + verb-ing. Negative: am not/isn’t/aren’t + -ing. Questions: Are you working?
grammar.examples: I’m studying right now. / They aren’t sleeping.
grammar.translation: Estou estudando agora. / Eles não estão dormindo.
grammar.usage: Choose -ing for an action in progress, not a routine.
grammar.errorExplanation: Present continuous needs be + -ing.

grammar.title: Simple present vs present continuous
grammar.explanation: Contrast regular habits/facts with actions in progress or temporary situations.
grammar.form: Simple present: often/every day/usually. Present continuous: now/at the moment/this week.
grammar.examples: He works downtown. / He’s working from home this week.
grammar.translation: Ele trabalha no centro. / Ele está trabalhando de casa esta semana.
grammar.usage: Some state verbs (like, know, want) are not normally continuous at this level.
grammar.errorExplanation: Use simple present for a general preference.

workbook.question: Why don’t we ___ a taxi?
workbook.explanation: Suggestion: Why don’t we + base verb.

grammar.title: Object pronouns
grammar.explanation: Use an object pronoun after a verb or preposition to refer to the receiver of an action.
grammar.form: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. Subject: I like him. Object: He likes me.
grammar.examples: I know her. / Can you help us?
grammar.translation: Eu a conheço. / Você pode nos ajudar?
grammar.usage: Object pronouns do not normally come before the verb as the subject.
grammar.errorExplanation: Use me after likes, not I.

grammar.title: Like + verb-ing
grammar.explanation: Use like/love/hate/enjoy + -ing to talk about activities and preferences.
grammar.form: like/love/hate/enjoy + verb-ing; question: Do you like dancing?
grammar.examples: I love listening to music. / He hates waiting.
grammar.translation: Adoro ouvir música. / Ele odeia esperar.
grammar.usage: Do not use the infinitive in this target pattern after enjoy.
grammar.errorExplanation: Enjoy is followed by -ing.

grammar.title: BE and DO review
grammar.explanation: Choose be for identity/state/location and do/does for simple-present actions and questions.
grammar.form: Be: Are you ready? Is she at home? Do/does + base verb for action questions: Do they play?
grammar.examples: Are you tired? / Do you play guitar?
grammar.translation: Você está cansado? / Você toca violão?
grammar.usage: Don’t use do to form a question with be.
grammar.errorExplanation: Invert the form of be to make its question.

vocabulary.example: My grandfather told us a tale.

grammar.title: Was / were
grammar.explanation: Use the past of be for past states, locations and descriptions.
grammar.form: I/he/she/it was; you/we/they were. Negative: wasn’t/weren’t. Questions: Was she…? Were they…?
grammar.examples: I was at home yesterday. / They weren’t ready.
grammar.translation: Eu estava em casa ontem. / Eles não estavam prontos.
grammar.usage: Use was/were, not did, to make questions with be.
grammar.errorExplanation: Past be makes questions by inversion.

grammar.title: Simple past: regular verbs
grammar.explanation: Use the simple past for completed events in the past.
grammar.form: Regular verbs: base + -ed; spelling changes: live→lived, study→studied, stop→stopped. Negative/question: didn’t/did + base verb.
grammar.examples: We watched a film. / She didn’t study last night.
grammar.translation: Assistimos a um filme. / Ela não estudou ontem à noite.
grammar.usage: After did/didn’t, the main verb returns to base form.
grammar.errorExplanation: Did already marks the past.

grammar.title: Simple past: irregular verbs
grammar.explanation: Common verbs have irregular past forms which must be learned.
grammar.form: go/went, have/had, get/got, see/saw, take/took, buy/bought. Use did/didn’t for questions and negatives.
grammar.examples: I went to a party. / He didn’t see the message.
grammar.translation: Fui a uma festa. / Ele não viu a mensagem.
grammar.usage: Irregular affirmative forms change, but questions use did + base verb.
grammar.errorExplanation: Didn’t is followed by the base verb.

grammar.title: Simple past review
grammar.explanation: Combine regular and irregular past forms to narrate a sequence of completed events.
grammar.form: Affirmative: subject + past form. Negative: subject + didn’t + base. Question: Did + subject + base?
grammar.examples: The detective arrived and found a note. / Did they leave early?
grammar.translation: O detetive chegou e encontrou um bilhete. / Eles saíram cedo?
grammar.usage: Use past form only in affirmative statements; after did use base form.
grammar.errorExplanation: Did carries the past tense.

grammar.title: There is / are; some / any
grammar.explanation: Describe what exists now and refer to an unspecified quantity.
grammar.form: There is + singular/uncountable; there are + plural. Some mainly affirmative; any often questions/negatives.
grammar.examples: There is a key on the table. / Are there any clues?
grammar.translation: Há uma chave na mesa. / Há pistas?
grammar.usage: Use are with plural nouns and any in many questions/negatives.
grammar.errorExplanation: Two doors is plural.

grammar.title: There was / were; place and movement prepositions
grammar.explanation: Describe what existed in the past and locate or trace movement.
grammar.form: There was + singular; there were + plural. Place: under, behind, between, next to. Movement: into, out of, across, through.
grammar.examples: There was a noise upstairs. / He walked through the hall.
grammar.translation: Houve um barulho no andar de cima. / Ele atravessou o corredor.
grammar.usage: Use into for movement to the inside; in describes location.
grammar.errorExplanation: Into emphasizes movement toward the inside.

grammar.title: Countable and uncountable nouns
grammar.explanation: Distinguish items that can be counted from substances or concepts treated as a mass.
grammar.form: Countable: an apple, two apples. Uncountable: rice, water, information. a/an with singular countables; some with plural/uncountable in affirmative clauses.
grammar.examples: I’d like an apple and some rice. / We need some water.
grammar.translation: Quero uma maçã e um pouco de arroz. / Precisamos de água.
grammar.usage: Do not use a/an directly with uncountable nouns.
grammar.errorExplanation: Information is uncountable.

grammar.title: Much / many / a lot of
grammar.explanation: Ask and answer about quantities.
grammar.form: How much + uncountable? How many + plural countable? A lot of works with both. Much/many common in questions and negatives.
grammar.examples: How much milk do we need? / How many eggs are there?
grammar.translation: De quanto leite precisamos? / Quantos ovos há?
grammar.usage: Many goes with countable plurals; much with uncountables.
grammar.errorExplanation: Apples are countable.

grammar.title: Comparative adjectives
grammar.explanation: Compare two people, places or things.
grammar.form: Short adjective + -er + than; y→ier; long adjectives: more + adjective + than. Irregular: good-better, bad-worse.
grammar.examples: This café is cheaper than that one. / Today is better than yesterday.
grammar.translation: Este café é mais barato que aquele. / Hoje está melhor que ontem.
grammar.usage: Use than for the second item in a direct comparison.
grammar.commonError: This meal is more cheap than that one.
grammar.correction: This meal is cheaper than that one.
grammar.errorExplanation: Cheap normally takes -er.

grammar.title: Superlative adjectives
grammar.explanation: Identify the highest/lowest degree within a group.
grammar.form: the + adjective-est for many short adjectives; the most + long adjective. Irregular: good→best, bad→worst. Often followed by in + place/group.
grammar.examples: It’s the oldest building in town. / This is the most expensive hotel.
grammar.translation: É o prédio mais antigo da cidade. / Este é o hotel mais caro.
grammar.usage: Superlatives generally require the before the adjective.
grammar.errorExplanation: Use the with a superlative.

grammar.title: Be going to: plans and intentions
grammar.explanation: Talk about a plan or intention decided before speaking.
grammar.form: Subject + am/is/are + going to + base verb. Questions: Are you going to travel?
grammar.examples: We’re going to visit Lima in June. / I’m not going to drive.
grammar.translation: Vamos visitar Lima em junho. / Não vou dirigir.
grammar.usage: Going to is followed by the base verb, not -ing.
grammar.commonError: She is going to visiting Rome.
grammar.correction: She is going to visit Rome.
grammar.errorExplanation: Use base verb after going to.

grammar.title: Be going to: predictions
grammar.explanation: Predict a future result using present evidence.
grammar.form: am/is/are + going to + base verb. Add time expressions such as soon, tomorrow, next week.
grammar.examples: Look at those clouds. It’s going to rain. / You’re going to love this city.
grammar.translation: Olhe aquelas nuvens. Vai chover. / Você vai adorar esta cidade.
grammar.usage: Use be going to for an evidence-based prediction as well as a plan.
grammar.errorExplanation: The form of be is required.

grammar.title: Adverbs of manner and modifiers
grammar.explanation: Adverbs explain how an action happens; modifiers strengthen or soften adjectives/adverbs.
grammar.form: Many adverbs: adjective + -ly (slow→slowly; careful→carefully). Irregular: good→well. Modifiers: very, really, quite, too.
grammar.examples: She speaks slowly. / He plays really well.
grammar.translation: Ela fala devagar. / Ele toca muito bem.
grammar.usage: Good is an adjective; well is commonly the adverb for performance.
grammar.errorExplanation: Use well to describe how he speaks.

grammar.title: Verbs + infinitive
grammar.explanation: Certain verbs are followed by to + base verb to express plans, hopes, decisions or needs.
grammar.form: want/need/hope/plan/decide/learn + to + base verb.
grammar.examples: I hope to visit Japan. / We decided to stay home.
grammar.translation: Espero visitar o Japão. / Decidimos ficar em casa.
grammar.usage: Learn the verb pattern; enjoy is normally followed by -ing, not to-infinitive.
grammar.errorExplanation: Decide is followed by to + base verb.

grammar.title: The or no article
grammar.explanation: Use the with specific, familiar or uniquely identified nouns; omit it in many general expressions.
grammar.form: the + specific noun; usually no the with languages, most countries, meals and general plural nouns.
grammar.examples: The phone on the table is mine. / I speak English.
grammar.translation: O celular sobre a mesa é meu. / Eu falo inglês.
grammar.usage: Do not add the before most country names or languages.
grammar.errorExplanation: Language names usually have no article.

grammar.title: Present perfect and past participles
grammar.explanation: Use the present perfect for life experiences or events connected to the present when the exact past time is not the focus.
grammar.form: have/has + past participle. I/you/we/they have; he/she/it has. Negatives: haven’t/hasn’t. Questions: Have you ever…?
grammar.examples: I’ve visited Mexico. / She hasn’t tried sushi.
grammar.translation: Já visitei o México. / Ela nunca experimentou sushi.
grammar.usage: Use a past participle after have/has, not the simple past form unless forms coincide.
grammar.errorExplanation: Go → went (past), gone (past participle).

grammar.title: Present perfect vs simple past
grammar.explanation: Choose present perfect for unspecified experience/current relevance; simple past with a finished, stated time.
grammar.form: Present perfect: have/has + participle, often ever/never/just/already/yet. Simple past: yesterday, in 2022, last week.
grammar.examples: Have you ever been to Chile? / I went in 2022.
grammar.translation: Você já esteve no Chile? / Fui em 2022.
grammar.usage: Do not normally combine present perfect with a finished time such as yesterday.
grammar.errorExplanation: A finished time calls for the simple past.

grammar.title: Question formation review
grammar.explanation: Build accurate yes/no and wh- questions across be, do, can, past be and present perfect.
grammar.form: Be: Are you…? Do: Do you work…? Can: Can you…? Past be: Were they…? Present perfect: Have you…?
grammar.examples: Where do you live? / Have you ever flown alone?
grammar.translation: Onde você mora? / Você já viajou de avião sozinho?
grammar.usage: Select the auxiliary that matches the tense/verb; avoid double auxiliaries.
grammar.commonError: Did you have ever been there?
grammar.errorExplanation: Present-perfect questions begin with have/has.

chunks.use: Talk about an experience not had.
chunks.example: I’ve never been to Africa.

chunks.phrase: Yes, I have. / No, I haven’t.
chunks.example: Have you tried it? — No, I haven’t.

chunks.phrase: It was the first time I…
chunks.meaning: Foi a primeira vez que eu…
chunks.example: It was the first time I flew alone.

chunks.use: Say an expected action has not happened so far.
chunks.example: Have you packed? — Not yet.
chunks.translation: Já fez as malas? — Ainda não.

studentBook.explanation: Past participle of go is gone; “been to” is common for visited-and-returned.

studentBook.question: I haven’t finished ___. (yet)
studentBook.explanation: Yet is common in present-perfect negatives.

workbook.question: Which is a past participle?
workbook.explanation: Go/went/gone: base/past/participle.

workbook.question: “Have you ever…?” asks about…
workbook.explanation: Ever is common when asking if an experience occurred at any point.

workbook.question: Choose the correct short answer. “Has she arrived?”
workbook.explanation: Repeat the auxiliary has in the short answer.

workbook.question: Which time expression usually pairs with simple past?
workbook.explanation: Last night is a finished past time.

workbook.question: We have ___ this film before. (see)
workbook.explanation: See → saw → seen.

workbook.question: They ___ not arrived yet.
workbook.explanation: They have not arrived yet / They haven’t arrived yet.
